item.title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2610.37407v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations. A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral. The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Ber\'anek

item.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2610.37635v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so H{\aa}stad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-\Omega(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.
item.dc:creator: Atul Mantri

item.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
item.description: arXiv:2610.37657v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.

item.title: SemDiff: Binary Similarity Detection by Diffing Key-Semantics Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2308.01463v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Binary similarity detection is a critical technique that has been applied in many real-world scenarios where source code is not available, e.g., bug search, malware analysis, and code plagiarism detection. Existing works are ineffective in detecting similar binaries in cases where different compiling optimizations, compilers, source code versions, or obfuscation are deployed. We observe that all the cases do not change a binary's key code behaviors although they significantly modify its syntax and structure. With this key observation, we extract a set of key instructions from a binary to capture its key code behaviors. By detecting the similarity between two binaries' key instructions, we can address well the ineffectiveness limitation of existing works. Specifically, we translate each extracted key instruction into a self-defined key expression, generating a key-semantics graph based on the binary's control flow. Each node in the key-semantics graph denotes a key instruction, and the node attribute is the key expression. To quantify the similarity between two given key-semantics graphs, we first serialize each graph into a sequence of key expressions by topological sort. Then, we tokenize and concatenate key expressions to generate token lists. We calculate the locality-sensitive hash value for all token lists and quantify their similarity. %We implement a prototype, called SemDiff, consisting of two modules: graph generation and graph diffing. The first module generates a pair of key-semantics graphs and the second module diffs the graphs. Our evaluation results show that overall, SemDiff outperforms state-of-the-art tools when detecting the similarity of binaries generated from different optimization levels, compilers, and obfuscations. SemDiff is also effective for library version search and finding similar vulnerabilities in firmware.
item.dc:creator: Zian Liu, Xiaoxi Meng, Viet Vo, Siqi Ma, Chao Chen, Dongxi Liu, Jun Zhang, Shigang Liu, Muhammad Ejaz Ahmed, Yang Xiang

item.title: DYNASHIELD: A Black-Box Moving Target Defense for LLMs via Dynamic Decoding Customization
item.description: arXiv:2412.07672v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks in which adversarial prompts induce harmful outputs. Existing defenses often require access to the model internals or additional training, limiting their applicability for service providers deployed through black-box APIs. In this paper, we propose DYNASHIELD, a moving target defense framework that improves robustness by customizing decoding hyperparameters and system prompts at inference time. DYNASHIELD includes two key steps: (1) it identifies decoding configurations that reduce attack success probability, and (2) it probabilistically samples from a weighted configuration pool to introduce controlled variability in model behavior. We evaluate DYNASHIELD across 7 open-source LLMs under 4 state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks, using adversarial prompts from AdvBench. Results show substantial reductions in attack success rate compared with 7 baseline defenses, while maintaining response quality and incurring minimal inference overhead. Because DYNASHIELD operates solely through exposed runtime controls, it requires no retraining or model-internal access. These results suggest that safety-aware dynamic decoding is a promising and practically lightweight defense mechanism for black-box LLM deployments.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoqun Liu, Weiming Qi, Qiben Yan

item.title: On the Reliability and Stability of Selective Methods in Malware Classification Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2505.22843v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The performance figures of modern drift-adaptive malware classifiers appear promising, but does this translate to genuine operational reliability? The standard evaluation paradigm primarily focuses on baseline performance metrics, neglecting confidence-error alignment and operational stability. While prior works established the importance of temporal evaluation and introduced selective classification in malware classification tasks, we take a complementary direction by investigating whether malware classifiers maintain reliable and stable confidence estimates under distribution shifts and exploring the tensions between scientific advancement and practical impacts when they do not. We propose Aurora, a framework to evaluate malware classifiers based on their confidence quality and operational resilience. Aurora subjects the confidence profile of a given model to verification to assess the reliability of its estimates. Unreliable confidence estimates erode operational trust, waste valuable annotation budgets on non-informative samples for active learning, and leave error-prone instances undetected in selective classification. Aurora is further complemented by a set of metrics designed to go beyond point-in-time performance, striving towards a more holistic assessment of operational stability throughout temporal evaluation periods. The fragility we observe in SOTA frameworks across datasets of varying drift severity suggests it may be time to revisit the underlying assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Herzog, Aliai Eusebi, Lorenzo Cavallaro

item.title: BadTime: An Effective Backdoor Attack on Multivariate Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2508.04189v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multivariate long-term time series forecasting (MLTSF) models are increasingly deployed in critical domains such as climate, finance, and transportation. Despite their growing importance, the security of MLTSF models against backdoor attacks remains entirely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose BadTime, the first effective backdoor attack tailored for MLTSF. BadTime can manipulate hundreds of future predictions toward a target pattern by injecting a subtle trigger. BadTime addresses two key challenges that become particularly severe in MLTSF: (i) the rapid dilution of local triggers over long horizons, and (ii) the extreme sparsity of backdoor signals under stealth constraints. To counter dilution, BadTime leverages inter-variable correlations, temporal lags, and data-driven initialization to design a distributed, lag-aware trigger whose influence persists over long-range forecasts. To overcome sparsity, it mixes label-similar and label-dissimilar poisoned samples and adopts a decoupled backdoor training objective that explicitly up-weights the sparse backdoor signal, enabling reliable learning at a poisoning rate as low as 1%. Extensive experiments show that BadTime significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art backdoor attack on time series forecasting by extending the attackable horizon from at most 12 timesteps to 720 timesteps (a 60x improvement) and reducing the MAE on target variables by 57% on average, while changing the average clean forecasting error by less than 1%.
item.dc:creator: Kunlan Xiang, Haomiao Yang, Wenbo Jiang, Haoxin Wang, Shiyue Huang, Shaofeng Li, Yijing Liu, Ji Guo

item.title: RHINO: Guided Reasoning for Mapping Network Logs to Adversarial Tactics and Techniques with Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2510.14233v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) generate vast volumes of low-level alerts that remain semantically fragmented, requiring labor-intensive manual correlation with high-level adversarial behaviors. Existing automation, namely rule-based systems and machine learning classifiers, has critical limitations: rule-based approaches fail to adapt to novel attack variations, while machine learning methods lack contextual awareness and treat tactic-technique (TT) mapping as syntactic matching rather than reasoning. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in cybersecurity, preliminary experiments reveal that existing LLM-based methods frequently hallucinate technique-tactic pairs or produce decontextualized mappings due to single-step classification. We introduce RHINO, a framework that decomposes LLM-based attack analysis into three structured phases: (1) behavioral abstraction, translating raw logs into contextualized narratives; (2) partitioned inference over the ATT&CK tactic space, generating candidate techniques by evaluating behavioral evidence against MITRE ATT&CK knowledge; and (3) knowledge-grounded refinement, cross-referencing predictions with official MITRE definitions to reduce hallucinations. We evaluate RHINO on three benchmarks (DAPT2020, CICIDS2017, IoT23) across four backbone models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4, and DeepSeek V3). Under a scenario-documented single-label formulation covering 11 distinct techniques, RHINO achieves an average top-1 accuracy of 87.34% under micro-averaging and 63.77% under macro-averaging, surpassing the strongest baseline by 16.78 and 13.60 points respectively. These results show that structured LLM reasoning can effectively translate low-level network observations into high-level adversarial behaviors.
item.dc:creator: Fanchao Meng, Jiaping Gui, Yunbo Li, Yue Wu

item.title: Cross-User Poisoning: User-Task Boundary Failures in Multi-User Collaborative Language Agents
item.description: arXiv:2511.17671v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language agents are moving from single-user assistants to shared collaborators in workspaces, forums, and group chats. A shared agent observes interleaved messages from multiple users, maintains persistent context, and executes tool actions, creating a boundary problem absent from standard single-user agents: the agent must decide not only whether an instruction is safe, but which user or task it is allowed to govern. We identify cross-user poisoning (CUP), where an adversary injects a message into shared context that is later applied while the agent serves a benign user, causing unauthorized actions or responses outside the instruction's intended scope. We validate CUP on two deployed multi-user agents, Continua and ElizaOS, and introduce MURMUR, a framework for evaluating shared-context agents under concurrent multi-user interactions. Across Slack, Workspace, and Airline domains, CUP achieves high attack success, persists across later interactions, and remains substantially more effective than matched prompt-injection attacks. We evaluate boundary-scoping defenses and find that context summarization alone is insufficient, while task clustering and provenance prompting substantially reduce non-adaptive propagation. These results show that robust multi-user agents require explicit user/task scoping rather than generic input filtering or context compression.
item.dc:creator: Atharv Singh Patlan, Peiyao Sheng, S. Ashwin Hebbar, Prateek Mittal, Pramod Viswanath

item.title: SELF: A Robust Singular Value and Eigenvalue Approach for LLM Fingerprinting
item.description: arXiv:2512.03620v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safeguarding the Intellectual Property (IP) of Large Language Models (LLMs) against model theft represents a critical challenge in contemporary AI research. Although fingerprinting is essential for establishing forensic evidence for model derivation, existing methods are susceptible to false claim attacks, weight manipulations, or high false positive rates, undermining their utility. To overcome these limitations, we propose SELF, \rev{a novel intrinsic weight-based fingerprinting scheme tailored for robust IP forensics via adversarial model lineage verification}. SELF eliminates dependency on input and inherently resists false claims, achieving robust \rev{provenance detection} through unique, scalable and transformation-invariant fingerprint extraction via singular value and eigenvalue decomposition of LLM attention weights. Experimental results demonstrate that SELF maintains high IP infringement detection accuracy while significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in reducing false positives and showing strong robustness against various downstream modifications, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/HanxiuZhang/SELF_v4.
item.dc:creator: Hanxiu Zhang, Qiang Xu, Yue Zheng

item.title: AgentSentry: Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents via Temporal Causal Diagnostics and Context Purification
item.description: arXiv:2602.22724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents aggregate dialogue history, tool outputs, and retrieved content into an accumulated runtime state to complete multi-step tasks. This execution model exposes agents to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which attacker-controlled instructions embedded in external artifacts enter the agent state and later influence tool use. Multi-turn IPI is especially challenging because injected content can persist across steps and trigger unauthorized state-changing actions only after merging with user intent. This creates a source-attribution problem: existing inference-time defenses can often detect suspicious behavior but do not directly distinguish whether a pending action is supported by the user task or influenced by injected content. They therefore resort to conservative blocking, termination, or broad filtering. We propose AgentSentry, an inference-time defense that operationalizes temporal causal diagnostics through boundary-local counterfactual re-executions at tool-return boundaries. It substitutes the mediator under a restored snapshot, records whether the pending proposal survives, and aggregates user-view and probe scores across adjacent boundaries. When a proposal is mediator-sensitive, AgentSentry purifies the implicated mediator content while preserving task-relevant evidence and resumes execution from the sanitized state. We evaluate AgentSentry on AgentDojo across four task suites, three IPI attack families, and three black-box LLM backbones. It records no observed successful attack in the evaluated cases (ASR = 0%) and achieves an average Utility Under Attack (UA) of 76.10%. Over the strongest evaluated baseline, it improves average UA by 1.84--7.60 percentage points, with benign FPRs of 2.06%--5.15%. We further evaluate long-horizon and adaptive attacks, imperfect purification, runtime overhead, and an OpenClaw case study.
item.dc:creator: Tian Zhang, Yiwei Xu, Juan Wang, Keyan Guo, Xiaoyang Xu, Bowen Xiao, Quanlong Guan, Jinlin Fan, Jiawei Liu, Zhiquan Liu, Hongxin Hu

item.title: LineageMark: Multi-user White-box Watermarking for Contribution Tracing in Model Derivation Chains
item.description: arXiv:2606.17123v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In open large language model (LLM) ecosystems, models are frequently adapted across multiple domains and applications, forming multi-stage derivation chains. Consequently, tracking and verifying historical contributions is essential for model provenance and intellectual property protection. However, existing watermarking methods are mainly designed for single-user, one-time embeddings, often fail under repeated model derivation and incremental updates. To address this problem, we propose LineageMark, a multi-user white-box watermarking framework for model derivation chains. The framework encodes watermarks in model parameters using a projection-based approach. Stable carriers are first selected to reduce sensitivity to model changes, each watermark bit is then represented as a projection statistic over these carriers. Additional watermark insertions introduce only bounded perturbations in the projection space, and margin constraints are used to maintain signal integrity. We evaluate the effectiveness of LineageMark in multi-stage model derivation chains. Experimental results show that LineageMark preserves contributor watermarks across multi-stage derivation and supports incremental multi-user watermark insertion. Furthermore, it exhibits robustness against perturbations such as re-watermarking, fine-tuning, quantization, and pruning.
item.dc:creator: Bingxue Zhang, Xiaofeng Xu, Feida Zhu

item.title: Deanonymizing Monero Transactions in Tor Network
item.description: arXiv:2607.07062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Monero is a privacy-focused cryptocurrency that deploys the Dandelion++ protocol and incorporates anonymity networks (such as Tor and I2P) to prevent malicious attackers from linking transactions with their source IPs. In this paper, we demonstrate that Monero's integration of the Tor network introduces a fundamental vulnerability: a Monero Tor node's originated transactions are exclusively forwarded to two outgoing Tor hidden service nodes (proxy nodes) prior to clearnet propagation, enabling an adversary to capture originated transactions by occupying the target node's outgoing connections. Based on this observation, we propose \textit{ProxyMark}, a three-stage deanonymization framework for the Monero Tor network, comprising node role identification, originated transaction identification, and node location deanonymization. Through experiments on the live Tor network, Monero mainnet, and testnet, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of \textit{ProxyMark} in successfully deanonymizing transactions originating from Monero nodes over Tor.
item.dc:creator: Ruisheng Shi, Shihan Zhang, Yulian Ge, Lina Lan, Qingfeng Zhang, Qin Wang

item.title: BioZKFHE: Scalable Encrypted Biometric Identification via Verifiable Homomorphic Similarity Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2607.22065v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large-scale biometric identification in outsourced settings requires two properties simultaneously: biometric templates and queries must remain protected during computation, and the encrypted similarity outputs produced by an untrusted compute node must be verifiably correct before any application result is released. Existing FHE-based biometric systems primarily address confidentiality, while practical verifiability introduces two bottlenecks in the underlying encrypted 1:N matching layer: rotation- and bandwidth-heavy similarity evaluation and the high cost of proving repeated homomorphic similarity traces. We present BioZKFHE, a framework for scalable encrypted biometric identification via verifiable homomorphic similarity evaluation that combines BGV homomorphic computation with committee-based threshold opening, verification, and decryption, and smart-contract enforcement of the committee's verification attestations. To reduce encrypted storage and avoid rotation-heavy encrypted 1:N matching, we propose Single-Coefficient Multi-Value (SCMV) packing, which binds multiple quantized embedding values into each plaintext entry through base-T expansion. To make proof generation practical, we propose Parallelizable and Verifiable Similarity Computation (PVSC), which exploits the Double-CRT execution structure of BGV to decompose each blockwise similarity trace into parallel proof instances that are opened and checked before result release. Under standard lattice assumptions and explicit committee/verifier assumptions, we analyze recoverability, noise growth, confidentiality, encrypted-output integrity, and finalized-result integrity. Experiments on FaceNet and MobileFaceNet show near-lossless biometric utility, up to 67% encrypted-storage reduction, and about 22-44 s end-to-end proof-verified runtime for 10k-40k templates.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing, early access, 23 July 2026
item.dc:creator: Rundong Xin, Taotao Wang, Xiaoxiao Wu, Weizhi Meng, Shengli Zhang, Shui Yu

item.title: Domain Decoupling Attack: Exploiting the Validation Gap Between Protective DNS and Shared Edge Routing
item.description: arXiv:2608.00643v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Command-and-control, data transfer, and censorship circumvention can hide in traffic to widely used services. DNS-bound access control grants permits based on resolved IP addresses, while shared edges route requests by tenant identity, creating a validation gap. An attacker can resolve an allowed anchor, obtain a permit for its shared edge address, and access a hidden tenant by presenting the tenant's name as both SNI and HTTP Host. To investigate this gap, we present the Domain Decoupling Attack (DDA), which exploits this gap in CDN and non-CDN hosting while preserving SNI--Host consistency. Across 1,069,048 domains, we conduct 18,025,068 successful probes. Overall, 95.8% of domains accept an external SNI, and 84.6% return content matching the named tenant. Exposure reaches 99.26% across 506,763 CDN domains and 92.75% across 562,285 non-CDN domains. The co-location graph places 666,413 exposed domains in cross-tenant components; 97.7% of 54,069 cross-tenant non-CDN addresses have a confirmed path to another tenant. None of the tested defenses bind tenant identity to the DNS-approved name. Cleartext inline IPS can block access based on SNI, but Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) hides it. The Windows Zero Trust DNS (ZTDNS) permit remains reusable in both cases, enabling the concealment of command-and-control and data-exfiltration traffic and facilitating censorship circumvention. The risk conceals command-and-control and data-exfiltration traffic and supports censorship.
item.dc:creator: Weizhe Wang, Minhong Dong, Jinhao Li, Lyuchuan Wei, Yao Zhang, Qiang Hu, Qi Guo, Guangquan Xu, Bin Wu

item.title: SynthGuard-ReleaseBench: Locked-Audit Evidence for Synthetic Tabular Data Releases
item.description: arXiv:2608.14753v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Synthetic tabular data are often judged by realism, privacy, or downstream-task scores. Those scores do not answer whether a proposed release is supported for a named use, population, and threat model. We introduce SynthGuard-ReleaseBench, an audit framework that locks the use, candidate panel, tolerances, and audit schedule before evaluation. It compares real-trained and synthetic-trained workflows on protected data, gives simultaneous finite-sample bounds for bounded loss gaps, requires controls, and keeps utility, empirical privacy risk, mechanism claims, and human release authority separate. Across four American Community Survey studies, five non-ACS records, two chronological diagnostics, and a sealed prototype, the benchmark retains favorable, unfavorable, and excluded outcomes. Transparent baselines pass some locked audits; compact learned models fail under the declared budgets; a health-table case is excluded because its negative control passes. A post-audit scaling arm, repeated across three generation seeds, shows the same locked criterion admitting those learned models once they are fit on enough data while still rejecting a dependence-destroying control at every size, so the criterion discriminates rather than merely rejects; the same repetition withdraws a finer single-seed ordering. The theory adds a pre-audit sample-size rule, variance-adaptive and anytime-valid certificates that tighten the bound two to ten times on the same locked evidence, a temporal certificate for time-ordered audits, and two lower bounds: ordinary bounded queries reconstruct a protected audit once the query budget reaches its size, and the panel-size correction is necessary rather than conservative. The contribution is a reproducible workflow for use-specific release evidence, not a claim that any generator is private, safe, or deployment-ready.
item.dc:creator: Jeffery Opoku, David Banahene

item.title: Defense-as-Skill: Evolving Runtime Guard Skill for Skill-Augmented Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.01487v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Skill-augmented agents load reusable skills as persistent runtime context, improving task performance but also giving malicious skills a durable channel for steering future actions. Such skills may leak secrets, corrupt code, bypass approvals, or stage data for exfiltration only after a concrete user task and workspace state make the unsafe action appear useful. This makes pre-install vetting insufficient and calls for runtime, task-conditioned protection. We propose Defense-as-Skill, a defense paradigm that implements the runtime guard itself as an installable, inspectable, and editable skill. Our guard, SkillSonar, runs alongside untrusted task skills and checks sensitive actions against the user's task boundary, routing each action to an allow, replan, or confirmation decision without modifying the underlying agent runtime. To study this setting, we construct SCOPE-R, a task-conditioned dataset covering 6 risk families and 21 sub-categories, with 206 attack-confirmed malicious instances and 43 benign tasks. We then improve SkillSonar on the SCOPE-R training subset using runtime guard-skill evolution, a Monte-Carlo Tree Search procedure that evolves the on-disk guard skill from feedback on the rollouts. Across Claude Code and OpenClaw, the evolved guard substantially reduces attack success while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off; on repeated GLM-5 runs, ID ASR drops from 0.482 to 0.104 and OOD ASR from 0.606 to 0.115, with gains transferring across victim models, held-out risk families, and external benchmarks. These results show that runtime guards can be skill-native, transparent, and evolvable policy artifacts for skill-augmented agents.
item.dc:creator: Xiaofang Yang, Ziqi Miao, Chen Qian, Dianbo Sui, Jing Shao, Lijun Li

item.title: Free-XOR TFHE via Lazy Bootstrapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.29983v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gate bootstrapping (GB) is a widely used technique in FHEW-like fully homomorphic encryption schemes, such as TFHE,for evaluating Boolean gates while simultaneously reducing the noise of the resulting ciphertext. However, the computational cost of GB is typically dominated by an expensive blind rotation (BR). [8] proposed a gate bootstrapping framework in which XOR gates can be evaluated simply by adding the two input ciphertexts, resulting in what they call freeXOR. To obtain a functionally complete set of operations, they further designed a GB procedure for evaluating AND gates using two lightweight blind rotations. In this work, we propose a similar gate bootstrapping framework that supports free evaluation of XOR gates while evaluating all symmetric binary Boolean gates, i.e., the 8 gates whose output is identical for the inputs (0,1)and (1,0), using two blind rotations. In addition to providing broader gate support, our construction is substantially simpler than that of [8], both conceptually and in terms of implementation. As a proof of concept, we implemented our approach and compared it with standard TFHE, measuring speedups of about 30% for AES and 34% for SHA.
item.dc:creator: Ali Ajorian, Osman Bi\c{c}er

item.title: Rank Ceiling for Twiddle-Perturbation Faults on the Forward NTT
item.description: arXiv:2610.30383v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ML-KEM and ML-DSA compute forward number-theoretic transforms on secret polynomials. Their fixed multipliers, or twiddles, are a documented fault-attack target. This paper characterises the linear map from a secret polynomial to the difference between correct and faulted transform outputs. Each selected twiddle takes a fixed changed field value at every use during one call; zero and nonzero replacements are covered. For one replacement, rank equals the number of butterflies sharing its twiddle, halving by layer from 128 to 2 for ML-KEM and to 1 for ML-DSA. With one replacement per layer, known fault positions, replacement values and a raw transform difference determine every coefficient except the constant and linear coefficients for ML-KEM, or the constant for ML-DSA. Lean 4 certifies this result for both 256-coefficient shapes over fields of characteristic other than two, with nonzero original twiddles. Those coefficients cancel from the difference for every allowed fault set and replacement choice. Seed storage motivates comparing a known correct public key with a released faulty key from the same seed. If only one ML-KEM secret-polynomial transform is affected and all other computations are unchanged, the decoded key difference is a known matrix column times the transform difference. An invertible column entry reconstructs the latter. For ML-DSA, reconstruction and exact candidate counts from paired compressed keys remain unestablished.
item.dc:creator: Chakshu Gupta

item.title: Combinatorial Lock for Trojan-Resilient AI Engines via Hash-Assisted Spectral Filtering
item.description: arXiv:2610.33437v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-trigger backdoor attacks, in which heterogeneous trigger mechanisms (e.g., patch, blend, warping, and the latent-domain Spy-Watermark) coexist within a single poisoned model, cannot be addressed by existing shortcut-based defenses that assume a single, static attack mechanism. Current multi-trigger remedies (BU+FT, BU+ANP, and BU+ABL) rely on backdoor unlearning, which incurs high training costs and loses effectiveness at low poisoning ratios. This paper proposes Combinatorial Lock, a training-free, reference-calibrated defense that reduces multi-trigger identification to a combinatorial problem over binary activation signatures. This formulation is the key novelty: it yields a multi-trigger defense that is training-free, trigger-oblivious, and directly implementable in hardware, since its decision rules can be evaluated with integer and logic operations. The framework combines anomaly-gated spectral scrubbing, which removes the malicious subspace only from inputs identified as anomalous, with a hash-compressed combinatorial signature verified by an ensemble of detection experts, including a compound-attack-aware expert for multi-trigger inputs. A joint threshold-shrinkage search identifies an operating point ($\tau$ at the 97.1st percentile, $\gamma = 0.78$) that reduces the attack success rate (ASR) to as low as 0.1% while preserving 97.8% clean accuracy. Evaluation on six models (ResNet18, VGG16, MobileNet, AlexNet, ViT-Small, ViT-Base) shows strong generalization: near-100% ASR drops to single digits across poisoning rates of 1-10% and 1-9 simultaneous triggers, with only gradual degradation in clean accuracy. ASIC and FPGA implementations confirm practicality, adding a consistent 19-20% latency overhead across all evaluated architectures and establishing Combinatorial Lock as a hardware-native approach to multi-trigger backdoor mitigation.

item.title: Attack logics, not outputs: Concept-based Property Attacks for Shortcut Elimination in Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.34923v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) for computer vision are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, such that minuscule malicious changes to inputs may induce unintuitive outputs. One key approach to verify and mitigate such robustness issues is to falsify expected output behavior, which enables local robustness guarantees and adversarial training. Due to the black-box nature of NNs, current attacks only falsify a class of the final output, such as flipping from $\text{stop_sign}$ to $\neg \text{stop_sign}$. In this work we argue that robustness analysis should focus more generally on logical inconsistencies in concept-level reasoning rather than solely on output misclassification. We formalize this perspective through concept-based properties, i.e., constraints over human-interpretable concepts such as $\text{red} \land \text{octogonal} \implies \text{stop_sign}$ and study the falsification of such properties as a principled form of adversarial attack. Furthermore, an implementation of concept-based properties on already trained NNs is proposed using techniques from concept-based explainable artificial intelligence (C-XAI). For that we formally prove that attacks on concept-based properties are expected to have a reduced search space compared to simple class falsification, whilst arguably be more aligned with intuitive robustness targets. The practical effectiveness of our approach for logically informed adversarial training is shown in an empirical study across multiple models and datasets, including both vision and a security-relevant code processing task. Our results demonstrate that concept-level falsification generalizes classical adversarial attacks: Retraining on our novel attacks maintains robustness gains as compared to classical adversarial retraining whilst better eliminating semantic biases.

item.title: False-Alarm Improvements and Detection Trade-Offs in Quantum Machine Learning for Intrusion Detection: A Reproducible Secondary Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.35235v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Published results in quantum machine learning for intrusion detection (QML-IDS) require joint interpretation of false-positive rate (FPR), attack true-positive rate (TPR), and evaluation provenance. We reconstruct operating points in the 25-entry frame selected by Kaissar and colleagues: 21 included articles, 20 identified documentary families, substantive methodological material consulted for 15, and 24 descriptive points from five. In one test-labelled comparison, a quantum support vector machine reduces FPR from 6.875% for random forest to 3.329%, while TPR decreases from 93.955% to 93.682%; both rates improve against three other comparators. In another study, a complete benign row identifies FPR as 12/6000 (0.200%), despite incomplete attack-side allocation that requires additional assumptions for TPR. Normalized matrices identify detection ranges rather than a unique aggregate rate. A uniform provenance rule separates training-described and test-adjusted results from six conditional illustrations whose independence remains unverified. The contribution is a reproducible interpretation of favorable comparisons and detection trade-offs, without converting descriptive results or hypothetical calculations into operational guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Fern\'andez-Barrios, Iker Pastor-L\'opez, Asier Gonz\'alez-Santocildes, Pablo Garc\'ia Bringas

item.title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2610.35532v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unsafe deserialization turns untrusted data into attacker-controlled execution, and a single vulnerability can admit diverse exploit variants that evade defenses tailored to a known exploit. Existing defenses typically operate at a single enforcement point with limited visibility into the full attack. Combining controls across layers offers complementary protection, but coordinating them to preserve legitimate functionality and adapting them to new variants requires substantial expert effort. We propose JANUS, a red-blue adversarial framework for automated cross-layer defense synthesis. Starting from a known exploit, \sys iteratively refines deployment-specific policies in an isolated offline environment. A black-box attacker probes the current policy for exploit variants using only externally observable feedback. The defender summarizes each verified variant into its security-relevant effects, uses counterfactual replay to separate complementary coverage from redundant enforcement, and jointly selects and scopes controls across layers. Each candidate policy is validated against accumulated exploits and benign workflows. We evaluate JANUS on sixteen vulnerability deployments across six Java and PHP applications against gateway, application, system, and cross-layer defenses. JANUS reduces held-out attack success to 6.2%, compared with 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, fully mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and preserves 98.4% of benign functionality tests at a 6.9% targeted P95 latency increase.
item.dc:creator: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie

item.title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35541v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Web services increasingly expose backend interfaces that let users delegate tasks to AI agents, which invoke service operations directly without navigating websites. This shift changes how existing Web vulnerabilities can be exploited. We investigate these changes through VELA, an executable benchmark covering 44 vulnerabilities across twelve Web application families. The benchmark preserves vulnerable backends and derives agent-facing interfaces from legitimate workflows. We evaluate three commercial agents across multiple interface configurations, using controlled comparisons to separate interface effects from agent behavior and independent oracles to verify attack outcomes. Our results show that the agent realizes every attack that direct interface invocation realizes in the reference configuration, so exploitability is set mainly by the interface: 91% of vulnerabilities remain exploitable under the reference design. Interface restrictions prevent some attacks by removing required operations or limiting input control, while retention remains high across vulnerability classes. No case-level loss in the reference configuration is attributed to agent refusal or input normalization, and in one case the agent completed an attack by supplying calls the attacker omitted. Across the tested configurations, interface design affects exploitability more than agent choice, moving retention from 39% to 95% against at most 4.5 points across agents, but some restrictive interfaces also limit legitimate workflows. Our study provides a systematic empirical account of how agent-mediated access reshapes existing Web vulnerabilities, grounding future Web architecture design in measured security outcomes and trade-offs between reducing attack exposure and preserving legitimate functionality in agent-facing services.

item.title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
item.description: arXiv:2610.35835v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

item.title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
item.description: arXiv:2407.04898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.

item.title: Differential Privacy of Decentralized Learning: Centralized Rate Conditions and Nearly Tight Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2505.19969v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We analyze the differential privacy of gossip averaging on a graph with independent Gaussian noise at every node, as seen by a subset of observing nodes. We characterize the privacy loss of any sensitive node over multiple gossip steps as that of a Gaussian mechanism whose sensitivity is the solution to a binary quadratic problem with a coefficient matrix determined by the gossip matrix. We recognize this matrix as a Toeplitz matrix plus a small correction, and show that its Toeplitz symbol controls how the DP guarantees grow with the number of steps. Under a computable condition on the Toeplitz symbol, the privacy guarantee matches that of a trusted central aggregator, and we give a utility bound for strongly convex learning problems that similarly matches the centralized case. Finally, we give numerical recipes for upper and lower bounds on the DP guarantees. On realistic test cases, the two bounds agree to within a few percent.
item.dc:creator: Antti Koskela, Tejas Kulkarni

item.title: Robust GNN Watermarking via Implicit Perception of Topological Invariants
item.description: arXiv:2510.25934v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) represent valuable intellectual property, yet watermarks based on out-of-distribution triggers can weaken under pruning, fine-tuning, and distillation. We present InvGNN-WM, which links ownership verification to graph-invariant prediction. By supervising a shared GNN backbone to predict normalized algebraic connectivity on owner-private carrier graphs, InvGNN-WM enables calibrated multi-bit black-box verification through either an auxiliary scalar endpoint or a fixed owner-side decoder of ordinary task logits. We provide conditional guarantees for task-loss control, decision preservation, and key separation, and prove NP-completeness of the exact-removal decision problem for a restricted class of monotone separable decoders. Experiments on node- and graph-classification benchmarks demonstrate high watermark fidelity with small changes in task performance. The task-logit deployment achieves higher detection rates than PreGIP-adapted in matched comparisons and retains detection under the evaluated extraction and retraining budgets. Watermark-assisted distillation further enables owner-side recovery using private verification material.
item.dc:creator: Jipeng Li, Yanning Shen

item.title: When AI Agrees Too Much: Manipulating Automated Code Review via Bias Injection
item.description: arXiv:2603.18740v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated Code Review (ACR) systems integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in software development workflows, ranging from interactive assistants to autonomous agents in CI/CD pipelines. In this paper, we study how LLM-based vulnerability detection in ACR is affected by the framing effect: the tendency to let the presentation of information override its semantic content in forming judgments. We examine whether adversaries can exploit this through contextual-bias injection (crafting PR metadata to bias ACR security judgments) as a supply-chain attack vector against real-world ACR pipelines. To this end, we first conduct a large-scale exploratory study across 6 LLMs under five framing conditions, establishing the framing effect as a systematic and widespread phenomenon in LLM-based vulnerability detection. We then design a realistic and controlled experimental environment, evaluating 33 CVEs across 20 real-world projects and two popular ACR pipelines (Claude Code and CodeRabbit), to assess the susceptibility of real-world ACR pipelines to vulnerability re-introduction attacks. We employ two attack strategies: a template-based attack inspired by prior related work, and a novel LLM-assisted refinement attack. We find that template-based attacks are ineffective and may even backfire, as direct biasing attempts raise suspicions. Our refinement attack, on the other hand, is successful in 32/33 (97%) cases, exploiting a fundamental asymmetry: attackers can iteratively refine attacks against a local clone of the review pipeline, while defenders have only one chance to detect them. Overall, our findings highlight the dangers of over-relying on ACR and stress the importance of human oversight and contributor trust in the development process.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Alexopoulos, Nikolaos Alexopoulos, Diomidis Spinellis, Dimitris Mitropoulos

item.title: Who Gets Flagged? The Pluralistic Evaluation Gap in AI Content Watermarking
item.description: arXiv:2604.13776v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Watermarking is becoming the default mechanism for AI content authentication, with governance policies and frameworks referencing it as infrastructure for content provenance. Yet across text, image, and audio modalities, watermark signal strength, detectability, and robustness depend on statistical properties of the content itself, properties that vary systematically across languages, cultural visual traditions, and demographic groups. We examine how this content dependence creates modality-specific pathways to bias. Reviewing the major watermarking benchmarks across modalities, we find that, with one exception, none report performance across languages, cultural content types, or population groups. To address this, we propose three concrete evaluation dimensions for pluralistic watermark benchmarking: cross-lingual detection parity, culturally diverse content coverage, and demographic disaggregation of detection metrics. We argue that watermarking is part of the pluralistic alignment pipeline and should be held to the same evaluation standards. We connect this to governance frameworks currently mandating watermarking deployment without requiring fairness evaluation. Our position is that evaluation must precede deployment, and that the same bias auditing requirements applied to AI models should extend to the verification layer.

item.title: TextCloak: Safeguarding Data from Unauthorized LLM Fine-Tuning via RL-Driven Unlearnable Examples
item.description: arXiv:2607.28862v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to significant advances across a wide range of language tasks, while simultaneously raising growing concerns about unauthorized online data exploitation and privacy leakage. Unlearnable examples (UEs) emerge as a promising defense by injecting crafted perturbations into data such that models trained on them exhibit degraded utility. However, existing methods for text protection are primarily designed for classification tasks and discriminative language models, which limits their broad applicability (e.g., instruction following or reasoning) in LLMs. In this work, we propose **TextCloak**, an RL-driven data synthesis framework that safeguards textual data against unauthorized LLM fine-tuning. TextCloak employs a *UE generative policy* that transforms clean text into unlearnable examples while preserving semantic fidelity and linguistic naturalness. To optimize the policy, we introduce **GRPO-UE**, which simulates the attacker's LLM fine-tuning and rewards downstream degradation via group-relative policy optimization. This overall formulates a bi-level optimization loop, allowing the generator to discover effective protective patterns. Comprehensive experiments on six publicly available datasets and nine state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that TextCloak consistently impairs unauthorized LLM fine-tuning while maintaining text utility for legitimate use. Further analyses confirm its transferability and robustness across model architectures, training configurations, and adaptive attacks, highlighting its broad applicability as a practical defense for online content.
item.dc:creator: Chengshuai Zhao, Pingchuan Ma, Dawei Li, Bohan Jiang, Zhiyuan Yu, Zhen Tan, Huan Liu

item.title: Coefficient choice in Galois-ring lifts of APN permutations: sharp unit-direction spectra and one-term optimal lifts
item.description: arXiv:2610.21178v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Permutation polynomials over the Galois ring $\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)$ are nonlinear components for symmetric primitives that add keys in the ring, as in secure computation modulo $2^k$. R{\o}njom and Sandrib showed that their differential uniformity is at least $2q^{k-1}$, where $q=2^m$. For the class studied here it is attained on top-layer differences, while almost all differences are units. We ask how small the difference table can be on unit differences when the residue permutation is fixed and only higher coefficient digits of its lift are chosen. Let $m\ge5$ be odd, $k\ge3$, and let $p$ be a reduced quadratic almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutation of $\mathbb{F}_q$ whose derivative is nowhere zero and two-to-one. Over all lifts of $p$, the least possible maximum on unit differences is $q$ or $2q$, decided by two invariants of $p$ and the level $k$. We describe every lift attaining it and show that the coefficients modulo $8$ decide optimality at every level. For every odd $m\ge5$, residue permutations with at most $16$ monomials attain $q$ after one $2$-adic digit of one coefficient of the natural lift is changed. For an explicit infinite family, one added monomial lowers the maximum on unit differences from $4q$, or from at least $q^2$, to $2q$ at every level without raising the degree. Under a uniform starting state and independent uniform round keys, valuation preservation yields layerwise bounds for characteristics and two-round differentials that distinguish lifts with the same global uniformity. Core results are formalized in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Hiroki Fukui

item.title: NetGuise: Adversarial Traffic Generation for Early-Stage Classifier Evasion
item.description: arXiv:2610.27456v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Early-stage encrypted traffic classifiers make decisions from only the first few packets of a connection, enabling low-latency classification but raising robustness concerns under realistic traffic morphing. Existing adversarial traffic generation methods often assume complete flows, feature-level perturbations, or iterative runtime feedback, which do not match the constraints of early-stage execution. We present NetGuise, a target-conditioned traffic morphing framework that generates packet-level padding and non-negative delay actions while preserving packet direction, ordering, and packet count and respecting MTU, bandwidth, and latency constraints. We evaluate NetGuise for censorship evasion under two observation interfaces, i) a history-only causal interface for online packet-by-packet execution, ii) and a full-window oracle interface that provides an upper-bound characterization of early-stage morphability. On VANT, NetGuise achieves 33.2% mean targeted evasion under the causal interface versus 82.0% under the oracle interface; on UTMobileNet, the corresponding results are 5.6% and 81.8%. NetGuise outperforms the strongest causal baseline, BAP, on both datasets and, on VANT, reduces bandwidth overhead from 19.80% to 3.02% and generation latency from 37.42 ms/flow to 1.16 ms/flow. Under the oracle interface, it achieves up to 85.7% targeted evasion, retains 43.5% after four rounds of adaptive censor retraining, and maintains 48% under zero-shot cross-environment transfer. Our results show that early-stage classifiers can remain morphable despite high clean accuracy and that robustness evaluation should account for targeted morphability, observation constraints, defender adaptation, and operational network conditions.
item.dc:creator: Binghui Wu, Dinil Mon Divakaran, Mohan Gurusamy

item.title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
item.description: arXiv:2610.30645v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.
item.dc:creator: Ruixuan Deng, Zhengfeng Ji, Jiayu Zhang, Li Zhou
